title: The verbal clause: order, subject and object

objectives.can: Find the verb, subject and object of a verbal clause and notice when something stands before the verb.

explanation.summary: A Hebrew verbal clause usually begins with its verb. The subject is already in the verb's ending; a noun or pronoun subject, if there is one, usually follows the verb, and the object follows after that. When something else stands before the verb, the writer is doing something with it. This lesson teaches how to find the parts and what to notice.

sections.heading: Start with the verb
body: In Hebrew prose the verb tends to come first in its clause. Read it first: its prefix or ending gives you the person, gender and number of the subject. A Qal qatal such as בָּרָא is third masculine singular, so the clause already says 'he created' before any noun appears.

The verbs in many narrative verses begin with וַ or וַיִּ, as in וַיִּיצֶר and וַיֹּאמֶר. These are narrative forms, taught in the next stage of the course. For now treat each as a verb with 'and' on the front and find its subject in the same way.

sections.heading: The subject
body: The subject may be only what the verb's ending says, 'he', 'she', 'they'. Or a noun or a name is added to say who it is. In the usual order the subject stands straight after the verb: in Genesis 1:1 the verb בָּרָא is followed by אֱלֹהִים, 'God'. In Genesis 2:7 the verb וַיִּיצֶר is followed by יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים. A pronoun used as the subject is not needed to show who acts, since the verb already does so; when it is there, it usually adds emphasis or contrast.

The subject agrees with the verb in gender and number. A feminine singular subject has a feminine singular verb; a plural subject, a plural verb. The agreement is often what tells you which noun is the subject when there are several nouns in the clause.

sections.heading: The object, and אֵת
body: A direct object follows the subject: in Genesis 1:1 it is 'the heavens and the earth', each introduced by אֵת. As you saw in the lesson on prepositions and the object marker, אֵת regularly marks a definite object, so it is a good signal: whatever follows אֵת is probably the object. In Genesis 4:1 the verb יָדַע is followed by אֵת and the name חַוָּה, the woman who is known.

The order is flexible. A prepositional phrase or an adverb may come between the verb and the object, as in the phrase לָהֶם in the first clause of Ruth 1:4, where the object נָשִׁים comes after 'for themselves'. The object marker and the endings let the reader see what is what, even when the order changes.

sections.heading: When something stands before the verb
body: The ordinary order, verb first, is often taken as the unmarked pattern. When a noun, a name or a pronoun comes before the verb, grammarians usually see a reason. The commonest ones are: a contrast between two subjects (Orpah kissed her mother-in-law, but Ruth clung to her); a new subject or a new topic, as when the story turns to someone else; a piece of background or description, as the first mention of the serpent in Genesis 3:1; and emphasis.

These are tendencies that grammarians have observed, not rules, and scholars disagree about how best to describe them. Do not try to decide the reason mechanically. First notice that something stands before the verb, then ask what the surrounding sentences are doing.

sections.heading: Agreement, and where it seems to fail
body: Hebrew has some well-known cases in which the verb does not agree in the way you would expect from the form of the subject. The word אֱלֹהִים has a plural ending but, when it means the one God, it takes a singular verb: in Genesis 1:1 the verb בָּרָא is singular. Some describe this as a plural of majesty or of fullness, though how best to explain it is discussed.

A collective noun, singular in form but meaning a group, can take a plural verb, as with הַצֹּאן 'the flock' in Genesis 30:39. And when a verb comes before a subject made of more than one person, it may agree with only the first, or with all. In Ruth 1:5 the verb is plural, matching the two sons that follow.

misunderstandings: Hebrew is not 'subject-verb-object' like English. The usual order of a verbal clause is verb first, then subject, then object.
A noun before the verb is not automatically the subject; always check the verb's gender and number and the object marker.
A plural-looking word with a singular verb is not an error. אֱלֹהִים with a singular verb is regular when the word names the one God.
A subject pronoun is not needed in Hebrew; its presence shows that the writer is doing something, such as contrasting two people.

deeper.heading: Word order and the reader's attention
body: Hebrew scholars have long noted that the first position in a clause is used for what is most important to the sentence. A fronted noun can point to a contrast, a change of subject, or a time or place that frames what follows. Which of these it is has to be decided from the passage, and sometimes it cannot be decided with certainty.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: IN THE beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The verb בָּרָא comes first after the adverbial phrase בְּרֵאשִׁית. The subject אֱלֹהִים follows it, and the object follows the subject: אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ. Although אֱלֹהִים has a plural ending, the verb is singular. The order verb, subject, object is the usual one.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: Then the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: וַיִּיצֶר is a narrative verb in the third masculine singular. The subject is יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים, the object is marked with אֶת: הָאָדָם. A further word, עָפָר, tells what the man was made from. The verb comes first, the subject second, the object third.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And the man knew Eve his wife; and she conceived and bore Cain, and said: 'I have gotten a man with the help of the LORD.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Here the subject, הָאָדָם, stands before the verb: וְהָאָדָם יָדַע. The writer turns to the man and the woman after the story of the garden, and the order helps to mark the turn. The verb is a qatal, and the object, the name חַוָּה, is marked with the object marker אֶת.

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: And they lifted up their voice, and wept again; and Orpah kissed her mother-in-law; but Ruth cleaved unto her.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two clauses side by side. In the first the verb stands first and the subject (Orpah) follows: וַתִּשַּׁק עָרְפָּה. In the second the subject stands before the verb: וְרוּת דָּבְקָה. The change of order sets Ruth against Orpah: one kissed her mother-in-law and left, the other clung to her.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And the flocks conceived at the sight of the rods, and the flocks brought forth streaked, speckled, and spotted.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: הַצֹּאן is a singular noun in form, 'the flock', but it names many animals. The verb וַיֶּחֱמוּ before it is masculine plural, and the second verb וַתֵּלַדְןָ is feminine plural. The agreement follows the meaning (the animals), not the singular form of the noun.

practice.prompt: Which word is the subject of בָּרָא?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: IN THE beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: אֱלֹהִים, which follows the verb
הָאָרֶץ
הַשָּׁמַיִם
בְּרֵאשִׁית
practice.explain: The subject normally follows the verb. אֱלֹהִים is the subject, and the verb is singular although the noun has a plural ending.

practice.prompt: What are the subject and the object of וַיִּיצֶר?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: Then the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The subject is עָפָר and the object is הָאָדָם
The subject is יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים and the object, marked by אֶת, is הָאָדָם
The subject is only the ending of the verb; there is no object
The subject is הָאָדָם and the object is יְהוָה
practice.explain: The subject follows the verb. The object marker אֶת stands before הָאָדָם, so it is the object, not the subject.

practice.prompt: What is noticeable about the position of הָאָדָם in this verse?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And the man knew Eve his wife; and she conceived and bore Cain, and said: 'I have gotten a man with the help of the LORD.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It is a vocative addressed to the reader
It is the object, placed first for emphasis
Nothing; it is the usual order of a Hebrew clause
The subject stands before the verb, which marks a turn of the story to the man and woman
practice.explain: A subject before the verb is unusual in narrative, and the grammarians see it as a sign of a new topic or a change of scene. הָאָדָם agrees with the verb יָדַע: both are masculine singular.

practice.prompt: Why does Ruth's name come before the verb in the second clause?

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: And they lifted up their voice, and wept again; and Orpah kissed her mother-in-law; but Ruth cleaved unto her.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: Hebrew always puts a name before the verb
It marks a contrast with Orpah in the first clause
It is a mistake in the text
It shows that Ruth is the object
practice.explain: In the first clause the order is verb, then subject (Orpah). In the second the subject comes first: וְרוּת דָּבְקָה. The writer is setting the two women against each other.

check.prompt: The verb וַיֶּחֱמוּ is plural, though הַצֹּאן looks singular. Why?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And the flocks conceived at the sight of the rods, and the flocks brought forth streaked, speckled, and spotted.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The noun is a collective: it names many animals, and the verb agrees with the meaning
The verb is wrong and should be singular
The verb has a different subject, hidden in its ending
The noun is in the construct state
check.explain: A collective noun can take a plural verb. The sense, many animals, decides the agreement.

check.prompt: The noun אֱלֹהִים ends like a plural. What is the number of the verb בָּרָא?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: IN THE beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It has no number
Plural, to agree with the noun
Singular: the word names the one God and takes a singular verb
Dual
check.explain: בָּרָא is third masculine singular. Where אֱלֹהִים names the one God, it regularly takes a singular verb; some describe the plural ending as a plural of majesty.

check.prompt: What is the effect of putting הַנָּחָשׁ before the verb in the first clause?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: Now the serpent was more subtle than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman: 'Yea, hath God said: Ye shall not eat of any tree of the garden?'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It introduces a new character and describes him, setting the scene for what follows
It turns the serpent into the object of the verb
It is the usual order of a verbal clause
It makes the clause a question
check.explain: The clause is וְהַנָּחָשׁ הָיָה עָרוּם. The subject comes first and the clause describes the serpent; it does not push the story forward. This is a common use of an initial subject.

check.prompt: In הַנָּחָשׁ הִשִּׁיאַנִי, what does the position of הַנָּחָשׁ suggest?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And the LORD God said unto the woman: 'What is this thou hast done?' And the woman said: 'The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The serpent is speaking
The clause is a question
The woman puts the blame on the serpent: the subject is set before the verb for emphasis and contrast
The serpent is the object of the verb
check.explain: The woman has been asked what she has done. Her answer begins with the subject before the verb: the serpent, not she, is the one who deceived. Grammarians read such an order as a contrast or a shift of attention.

check.prompt: Why is the verb וַיָּמוּתוּ plural?

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: And Mahlon and Chilion died both of them; and the woman was left of her two children and of her husband.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It is a plural of majesty
It agrees with the two sons that follow it, Mahlon and Chilion
It agrees with the woman in the next clause
It agrees with the word גַם
check.explain: The verb comes first and is plural, in agreement with the subject שְׁנֵיהֶם, 'both of them', who are then named: Mahlon and Chilion.

check.prompt: Rebekah's name stands before the participle in the first clause. What does that do?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Rebekah heard when Isaac spoke to Esau his son. And Esau went to the field to hunt for venison, and to bring it.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It means that Rebekah spoke first
It sets a new subject and a new scene: while Isaac speaks, Rebekah is listening; Esau's departure follows in the next clause
It is a question
It makes her the object of the participle
check.explain: A new subject before its verb (or here a participle) often turns the story to another person or scene. The following clause begins with the verb וַיֵּלֶךְ, and its subject עֵשָׂו follows.

check.prompt: Which word is the object of יָדַע, and how do you know?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And the man knew Eve his wife; and she conceived and bore Cain, and said: 'I have gotten a man with the help of the LORD.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: אִשְׁתּוֹ, because it has a suffix
חַוָּה, because the object marker אֶת stands before it
הָאָדָם, because it comes first
There is no object
check.explain: אֵת marks the object, and חַוָּה follows it. אִשְׁתּוֹ, 'his wife', is added to say who she is. הָאָדָם is the subject.

check.prompt: In וַיָּמָת אֱלִימֶלֶךְ אִישׁ נָעֳמִי, what is אִישׁ נָעֳמִי?

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: And Elimelech Naomi's husband died; and she was left, and her two sons.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A second verb
A phrase that says who Elimelech was: 'the husband of Naomi'
The subject, in front of the name
The object of the verb
check.explain: אֱלִימֶלֶךְ is the subject of וַיָּמָת, which follows the verb as usual. The words after it are in the construct state and describe him. The verb has no object, because 'die' takes none.

reading.why: The opening of Ruth sets one family on a plain stage: verbs come first, subjects follow, a pair of sons are the plural subject, and the one marked contrast is a good place to see what order tells the reader.

segments.title: Ruth
segments.english: AND IT came to pass in the days when the judges judged, that there was a famine in the land. And a certain man of Beth-lehem in Judah went to sojourn in the field of Moab, he, and his wife, and his two sons.

segments.title: Ruth
segments.english: And the name of the man was Elimelech, and the name of his wife Naomi, and the name of his two sons Mahlon and Chilion, Ephrathites of Beth-lehem in Judah. And they came into the field of Moab, and continued there.
